These other guys are staff officers. Again, he's angry at Furtula and wants Krstic to help him. And Krstic says very clearly, initially, Tosic and Sladojevic were heard wrong by the intercept operators, but it's clear as we go down the page that Krstic says, "I'll see what I can do, but it will disturb a lot. Please, you have some down at Nastic's and Blagojevic's." Well, Nastic is the commander of the Milici Brigade, the adjoining brigade to Bratunac, and Blagojevic is of course the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. Now, Mr. Blagojevic was not as silly as some of the commanders and wasn't on the radio speaking openly like these arrogant senior commanders were, but yet they used his name and clearly by using his name it's obvious that he is involved as is Furtula, as is all the brigade commanders, well involved and knowing about what is going on. Another interesting part of this: You'll see that Krstic says, "Well, take some from the MUP." And Beara says, "No, they won't do anything." Here's somebody that for some reason refused to take part. These are the Ministry of Interior people, so they're not as connected to the army as they might be, but they refused so. Whether it was out of moral conviction or because they were doing -- they were defending Zvornik, I don't know. But at the end Beara makes his intentions very clear, when he says, "There are still 3500 parcels that I have to distribute and I have no solution." And Krstic says, "I'll see what I can do." As you'll see, parcels is how the army referred to the prisoners. At one point Mr. Jokic in a conversation makes a slip and says, "We've been reporting on a number of people -- I mean, parcels since this morning." So you'll see it used over and over again, and then you'll see Mr. Jokic's slip. Clearly they're talking about human beings here. Security officers are working under commanders. The brigade commanders are keyed into this and the operation continues. If you could go to the -- this is a logbook from -- that reflects meetings of the Bratunac Brigade. We didn't have very many dates that survived the purge, but we did have October -- I believe this was October 16th. And when Momir Nikolic spoke up at this meeting, where Blagojevic is specifically present, he says, "We are currently engaged in tasks issued by the Army of the Republika Srpska General Staff (sanitation)." Well, the word "sanitation" is a rough translation of the Bosnian word "asanacija", which when you see the original you'll see. Asanacija is a military term out of the JNA lexicon that means "cleaning up after the battlefields" and principally has to the with recovering the bodies of men and animals and burying them. When they use asanacija in Srebrenica, they're talking about burying human beings. And this is a direct reference to the re-burial operation from the large mass graves right near the Bratunac Brigade headquarters to areas south of Srebrenica. This is clear from -- the evidence is clear from this statement. And Momir Nikolic will now confirm that. What this is is a very kind of simple-looking log. In each of the brigades they have what they call the forward command post, or under the VRS lingo, IKM, and it's where the command is based at the forward frontlines. It's a critical place. And in the case of Zvornik, it's up near Petkovci, and it's always manned by a senior officer because they're the ones that are looking down the barrels of the Muslim army. It's a critical position. And what this shows us is that Major Galic, one of the staff officers from the Zvornik Brigade, took over on an unscheduled duty change from Lieutenant Drago Nikolic at 2300 hours. Now, Drago Nikolic is the chief of the security for the Zvornik Brigade, and something at about 2300 hours or before got his attention and got him transferred unschedulely from the forward command post. We know from other Serb soldiers that what Drago Nikolic was assigned to do was go accept the prisoners as they came up from Bratunac that night and get them located in the schools. And this is something -- you don't change the duty officer at the forward command post without the knowledge of the commander. This is a critical job, a critical change. The commander is in the area. He's -- he is within communications at all times according to what he has to say himself. Many of his communications are hard-wired communications which are absolutely secure. Other communications that he carries with him have to go through a operations centre on a hill above Zvornik but are all linked in to the Zvornik Brigade and so he is under communications the entire time. And he'll tell you this -- or he told that to the OTP. So Mr. Obrenovic had to have been involved, had to have been informed of this major change that Drago Nikolic had to go deal with a huge job that was arriving, a mass of Muslims from Bratunac. This is a military police attendance log. That was another one of the logs that remained behind. And this shows that on the 14th of July several -- some ten military police officers, including their commander, Miomir Jasikovac, were assigned in a particular place. Now, you can't tell from this copy, but from the original you can see that there was a "0" written down -- an O, excuse me, and that O is erased. And on the back of the original there is a little legend and it says "T" means "terrain," "O" means "Orahovac." And "O" means "Orahovac" is also erased but you can clearly see it through the erasure marks and you can read the export reports on that. So the way this started out is that these people were marked as "O" on the 14th of July at Orahovac, ten of them including the commander, then in a purge somebody sloppily replaced the "O" and replaced it with a "T". You can see the same thing the next day where things were erased and an "R" was erased which we believe means "Rocevic." So we also now know from military police officers and others that the military police were present at Orahovac, and the most important thing about this is their commander was the one that was there. This is a commander that by Obrenovic's own words was a key player in helping set up the ambushes to deal with the Muslim column but that suddenly the night of the 13th disappears because he has a sore groin, according to Mr. Obrenovic. But then we see him in Orahovac taking charge of nine of his people, guarding Muslims, getting them prepared for murder. This is -- this is a point where the Muslims are approaching the Serbs and the Serbs need every man, every unit they have. And the military police is a bit of a cut above the rest because they have to keep -- one of their main jobs is to keep the troops in the trenches. So to have the commander of the MPs and nine of his people at Orahovac guarding Muslims is absolutely outrageous. He should have been guarding his families' security and his army's security and the ambushes in the woods with the others who were doing it. But his commander, Dragan Obrenovic, chose to put him there at that school. You've got 500 to 1.000 Muslims. If those Muslims escape and start running rampant in the town of Orahovac, where they are being held, that creates ungodly panic. If the soldiers at the frontline hear that their homes are being ransacked by Muslims, there are not going to be too many soldiers left on the frontlines. This kind of major assignment does not happen without the commander's knowledge. All right. When Pandurevic gets back, he gets back midday the 15th. He meets with Obrenovic. Obrenovic, who by definition and by command should know more about what's going on in this area than anybody else. A few hours after getting back and being briefed by Obrenovic and others, he sends a message to the Drina Corps command. Now, the first part of the message is about the horrible military situation that they're in, which I have already mentioned to you and I won't go over again. But these two separate paragraphs are the one time that we find in this entire record where someone is making direct reference to what's really going on. And he says, "An additional burden for us is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout the schools in the brigade area, as well as obligations of security and restoration of the terrain." Well, shortly after arriving Pandurevic obviously knows all about the Muslims in the schools. At the time of the writing of this, remember, everyone in Orahovac and Petkovci and Kozluk are dead, thousands of Muslims. He's been briefed by Obrenovic before writing, this yet Obrenovic says he doesn't know about anything until July 23rd, yet Obrenovic admits he's at the brigade headquarters on the 15th of July for a good part of the day, where this had to have been a major topic of discussion and interest and concern. Obligations of security. Well, we know that Beara, Mladic's Chief of Security, was running this murder operation. So when he says "obligations of security," what he means is guarding and murdering the prisoners. Restoration of the terrain. Again, that's the term Asanacija. And we know from the vehicle records, again the excavator operators themselves, by the time Obrenovic wrote this they had spent hours and hours and tonnes of fuel burying bodies. Then he says, "This command can not take care of these problems any longer, it has neither the material nor the resources. If no one takes on this responsibility, I will be forced to let them go." He still has some remaining at Pilica and Kula School, probably the 3500 that Beara is desperately trying to get resources to kill that very same day. I won't go into that any further, but that's a document you'll want to study. You'll want to study the expert reports and everything the Defence might have to say about that. Another intercept, this time with Mr. Jokic, looking for Beara, speaking to Beara, and at the bottom he says, "There are big problems, well, with the people -- I mean, with the parcel." That's what I referred to. Mr. Jokic is having to deal with Mr. Beara and dealing with the battalions that are holding the prisoners and sending the orders to the battalions that they be killed and dealing with the 4th Battalion, dealing with the 6th Battalion, dealing with 2nd Battalion. He's right in the centre of all this, and it's his communications that are key to the operation. One last intercept, where Jokic is talking to who we believe is General Miletic, the chief of the operations of the VRS Main Staff, and says, "Obrenovic is really engaged to the maximum. We all are, believe me. This packet has done the most to ruin us. And since this morning we've been reporting on the number of people." And then the general says, "Okay, don't talk to me about that." Now, they all are engaged to the maximum. The packet, or parcel - it's the same word in B/C/S - arrived that morning. This intercept was on the 14th of July. He's talking about this huge problem that he and Obrenovic and they all have with these, having thousands of Muslim prisoners dumped on them for the murder operation. And that's the last one of my critical documents that I've chosen to show you. And so I will conclude. Thank you for listening to me so patiently today. We'll begin our case with the testimony of Jean-Rene Ruez, the original lead investigator of this case. We'll continue chronologically through the witnesses, beginning in Potocari, moving into the events at Bratunac, Bratunac-Milici road, and Bratunac town, then we'll go to Zvornik, where you've heard most of the victims were murdered. We'll conclude with our military analyst, Rick Butler, who will help explain the key military doctrines and documents, intercepts and events, and he'll be assisted by General Patrick Cordingley, who is an actual brigade commander in the first Gulf War, who led troops in combat and at the same time captured several thousand Muslim prisoners and can talk to you what it's all about from a professional military man's position and where there are consequences for illegal action. We'll also in this case call a number of Serb soldiers, getting away from a traditional adversarial system. I would like you to see officers and soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade and the Bratunac Brigade. While many of them will not be telling the truth about various subjects, they will help you in the end to -- to consider and to review many of the important topics here. And I think you'll be able to identify most of the time when they're not telling the truth and when they are. One of the interesting things about lying is that many times you can figure out why someone's lying. For example, we see most of the Serbs from Potocari will never admit to you that there was any separations going on. What does that mean? That shows consciousness of guilt because they know that separations were part of the murder crime. But it will be unusual to hear from these men, but I think in the end it will be productive for you. For the next few months you will see the evidence in this case rise up, and it will envelope each of these defendants. You'll see that there's no secret security chain of command, there's no reason to exclude these officers from the murder operation, no consequences for these officers for following such atrocious orders. These accused and their troops were absolutely critical for the success to the murder operation and none of them had that the strength of character or courage necessary to say no and walk away. But unlike July 1995, today in this Tribunal there are consequences for this conduct. When you've see and reviewed all the evidence, I have no doubt that you will find each of the accused guilty as charged. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much for this very concise opening statement. As we planned, we'll hear the first witness tomorrow morning. So we are adjourned until tomorrow morning, 9.00, in the same courtroom.
